origin_region: Guangxi · Guilin (also Hangzhou in Zhejiang, Xianning in Hubei and Suzhou in Jiangsu)
cultivar: Osmanthus fragrans; the golden 'jin gui' and orange 'dan gui' types are the most fragrant
processing: The tiny flowers are shaken from the trees onto sheets in autumn, picked clean of twigs and dried quickly in shade or at low heat so they keep their colour and apricot scent; they are not fermented or roasted.
harvest_season: Autumn, late September to October, in a flowering window of only two or three weeks; the whole year's supply is dried then.
appearance_dry: Minute four-petalled florets a few millimetres across, golden-yellow to orange, loose and feathery.
appearance_wet: The florets swell slightly and float, releasing a strong apricot-and-honey scent.
taste_profile: Intense apricot, peach and honey perfume on a thin, delicate body; on its own it is all nose and little weight, which is why it is so often blended with tea.

brewing.notes: A level teaspoon per cup, water around 85 °C, 3 minutes; boiling water cooks the scent. Better still, add a pinch to a pot of green, oolong or black tea, or to ripe pu-erh. Keep the lid on.

vintage_note: Sold as the current autumn's flowers, usually in small quantities, and the colour tells you the age: fresh florets are bright gold and the scent is strong, while flowers more than a year old turn brown and smell of little. Chinese shops often state the harvest year and the origin (Guilin is the famous one). Sweetened or salted osmanthus in jars is a separate product for cooking, not for tea.
description:
Osmanthus is the small golden flower that perfumes Chinese cities every October, and dried on its own it makes one of the most fragrant infusions there is: apricot, peach and honey from a pinch of florets that weigh almost nothing. Guilin in Guangxi is the city most associated with it (the name literally means 'forest of osmanthus'), and Hangzhou and Suzhou have their own traditions.

There is barely any processing: the flowers are shaken from the trees during the short autumn bloom, cleaned and dried quickly and gently. Everything depends on that speed and on storage, because the scent is volatile and the colour fades from gold to brown within a year.

Brewed alone it is lovely but thin, a pale gold cup with a huge nose and not much body, so it is usually paired with tea: a pinch in green tea, oolong (osmanthus oolong is a scented tea in its own right) or black tea, or dropped into a pot of ripe pu-erh. Use water around 85 °C and keep the lid on; boiling water flattens the aroma.

Buy small amounts of the current year's flowers, bright in colour and strong in scent, and keep them sealed in the dark. It is inexpensive, and old stock is the only real risk.

Try a few florets in a cold brew of white tea, or in warm milk with a little honey; and if you like the scent, osmanthus oolong from Taiwan or Guangxi is the next step.
